title: FOMC Minutes — December 9–10, 2025
html:
Official minutes: HTML · PDF Local PDF: 2025-12-10 FOMC Minutes.pdf

Decision

The Committee cut the federal funds target range by a quarter point to 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent, the third straight cut. Interest on reserve balances fell to 3.65 percent and the primary credit rate to 3.75 percent. The vote was 9-3. Stephen Miran preferred a half-point cut. Austan Goolsbee and Jeffrey Schmid preferred no change, citing concern that progress toward 2 percent inflation had stalled in 2025 and that they needed more confidence inflation was falling sustainably. The Committee also judged reserves had reached ample levels and agreed to begin reserve management purchases of Treasury bills (and, if needed, Treasuries maturing in 3 years or less) "as needed." The aggregate limit on standing repo operations was removed.

Economic outlook

Staff said real GDP grew moderately this year; Q3 was solid, but the three-quarter average was slower than 2024. Staff expected the government shutdown to cut fourth-quarter growth by about 1 percentage point, with a matching boost in Q1 2026. Participants said activity was expanding moderately. Higher-income households drove much of the spending strength while lower-income households grew more price sensitive. Shutdown-related swings and delayed data made the underlying trend harder to read.

Inflation

Total and core PCE inflation were both 2.8 percent in September, higher than earlier in the year. Staff attributed the rise in core goods inflation largely to tariffs. A majority of participants noted that inflation had been above target for some time without moving closer to 2 percent over the past year. Longer-term expectations remained stable.

Labor market

Unemployment edged up to 4.4 percent in September, continuing a gradual rise since mid-2025. Payroll gains slowed in Q3 and hiring stayed subdued, though some indicators such as initial claims and job postings suggested more stability. The employment cost index rose 3.5 percent and average hourly earnings 3.8 percent over the year. Staff expected unemployment to decline gradually after 2025.

Financial markets & balance sheet

Reserves averaged around $2.9 trillion, about $500 billion below their level when runoff began in June 2022. Repo rates were elevated and volatile, and standing repo usage increased. The Desk projected reserve drops around year-end, late January and especially mid-to-late April (tax inflows to the Treasury's account), which could push reserves below ample without purchases. Survey respondents expected about $220 billion of net purchases in the first 12 months. Participants differed on front-loading purchases versus relying more on standing repo, and several wanted a more precise definition of "ample."

Risks participants flagged

  • Upside inflation risks remained elevated; some worried inflation could become entrenched and that more cuts amid high inflation could undermine credibility.
  • Downside employment risks had increased since mid-2025; most saw labor risks tilted to the downside.
  • A possible sharp rise in layoffs in a low-hiring environment, tariff pass-through, policy uncertainty and delayed data.
  • AI could raise growth without inflation but could also damp job creation.

What it signaled about next moves

Most participants expected further cuts if inflation declined as expected, but some suggested holding rates steady for a time after this cut. The minutes repeated that "monetary policy was not on a preset course." This was a Summary of Economic Projections meeting, with projections through 2028 released after the meeting.

Read-through for SPY

  • A third cut and new Treasury bill purchases added liquidity and lower short rates, supportive for equities heading into 2026.
  • Three dissents and talk of a pause signaled a slower pace of cuts ahead, limiting further rate-driven multiple expansion.
  • Rising unemployment and K-shaped consumer spending were risks to earnings breadth beyond the largest companies.
